To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) for most imputation functions, the best predictor of the outcome can be learned by first imputing, then predicting; (2) the best predictor is generally discontinuous, making it hard to learn; (3) the best imputation is not the one that perfectly imputes, but rather the one that preserves the conditional distribution of the outcome; (4) it is easier to predict the outcome jointly with the best imputation, rather than first impute, then predict

(i) for most imputation functions, imputation followed by a powerful learner is asymptotically optimal for prediction, (ii) the regression function on perfectly imputed variables is generally discontinuous and hard to learn, and (iii) joint learning of imputation and regression is easier than imputation followed by regression
(1) imputation and regression should be done jointly and (2) the best imputation function to do so is the identity.
